name: The Shepard Tone
statement: A tone that seems to rise forever yet never actually gets any higher.
statementAccent: seems to rise forever yet never actually gets any higher
meaning: The Shepard tone is an auditory illusion of a tone that seems to continually ascend or descend in pitch, yet ultimately gets no higher or lower. Often called an auditory barber pole, it is the sonic equivalent of an ever-rising staircase like those in Escher's drawings. It is named after the cognitive scientist Roger Shepard, who introduced it in a 1964 paper on the circularity of relative-pitch judgments, and its continuously gliding version, the Shepard-Risset glissando, was developed by the composer Jean-Claude Risset. The illusion is built from tones spaced an octave apart whose loudness is shaped so that the extremes fade away while the middle sounds loudest, making the pitch appear to move endlessly in one direction. It is a classic demonstration in psychoacoustics that pitch perception has more than one dimension, and it has been used in music and film scores to create a sense of unending rise.
mechanism: A Shepard tone is a sound made of a superposition of sine waves separated by octaves, for example one hundred hertz, two hundred, four hundred, eight hundred, and so on. Their loudness is weighted by a fixed, bell-shaped amplitude envelope: the components at the very high and very low ends are nearly silent, and those in the middle of the range are loudest. As the whole set of tones glides upward, the highest components fade out at the top while new ones fade in at the bottom, so no individual tone's beginning or end is noticed, and the spectrum is effectively cyclic. The listener perceives continuous upward motion, but because the pattern is circular, the tone never actually reaches a higher pitch. This works because pitch has two aspects: pitch height, how high or low a tone sounds overall, and pitch chroma or pitch class, its position within the octave, which repeats cyclically. The Shepard tone keeps the chroma clearly moving while the height stays ambiguous, exploiting the circular nature of pitch class.

examples.text: Sine waves an octave apart, weighted by a bell-shaped loudness envelope, fade in at the bottom as they fade out at the top, so the tone seems to rise endlessly.
Christopher Nolan's Dunkirk and the Batpod sound in The Dark Knight use Shepard tones to create a sense of ever-increasing tension or acceleration.
The looping music of Super Mario 64's endless staircase uses a modified Shepard scale, matching the visual illusion of a stairway going nowhere.

variants.name: The Shepard-Risset glissando
variants.text: Jean-Claude Risset's continuously gliding version, in which the pitch slides smoothly rather than in discrete steps, seeming to rise or fall without end.

variants.name: Pitch height versus pitch class
variants.text: The two-dimensional structure of pitch the illusion exploits: overall height, kept ambiguous, and cyclic chroma, kept clearly moving.

whyItMatters: The Shepard tone is a classic and vivid demonstration in psychoacoustics that pitch perception is not a single dimension but at least two: pitch height and the cyclic pitch class, or chroma. By keeping chroma moving while leaving height ambiguous, it produces the compelling illusion of endless ascent or descent, revealing how the auditory system can be systematically fooled and how it constructs pitch from spectral cues. Beyond the laboratory, the illusion has become a widely used tool in music and film, where composers and sound designers deploy Shepard tones and the Shepard-Risset glissando to evoke unending rise, mounting tension, or ceaseless acceleration, from Nolan's film scores to video-game music.

working.text: build a sound from sine waves an octave apart, so the components share the same pitch class across the range.
apply a bell-shaped amplitude envelope so the extremes are silent and the middle is loudest, hiding where tones enter and leave.
move the whole set in pitch, so the chroma seems to rise or fall endlessly while the overall height stays ambiguous.

limits: The Shepard tone is a constructed auditory illusion, not a natural sound, and it depends on the precise spacing of octaves and the shape of the amplitude envelope; imperfect construction weakens or breaks the effect. The illusion of endless motion holds because the spectrum is cyclic, but the perceived strength varies with the listener and the playback conditions. It demonstrates the two-dimensional structure of pitch for these special stimuli rather than proving that ordinary pitch perception is always so cleanly separable into height and chroma. And while the illusion is compelling, attentive listeners can sometimes notice the cyclic reset. So the Shepard tone is a carefully engineered demonstration of pitch circularity and the multidimensionality of pitch, powerful within its design but not a claim that all auditory perception behaves this way.
misreadings: The Shepard tone does not actually rise or fall without limit; its pitch is cyclic, so it only seems to move endlessly while its overall height stays the same. It is not a single pure tone but a stack of octave-spaced tones with a fixed loudness envelope, which is what creates the illusion. And it demonstrates the circularity of pitch class for specially built sounds, so treating it as evidence that pitch has no fixed height in general, or that the tone truly ascends forever, mistakes a clever construction for a property of all sound.
origin: Introduced by the cognitive scientist Roger Shepard in his 1964 paper on circularity in judgments of relative pitch, with the continuously gliding version developed by the composer Jean-Claude Risset.
